1.pericope_label: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the commandment of God our Saviour, and Lord Jesus Christ, which is our hope; Unto Timothy, my own son in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace, from God our Father and Jesus Christ our Lord.

schools.summary: Find the force of the claim in the preposition, since the idiom means by way of command, so that Paul writes as an apostle under orders; note that the title Saviour applies as properly to the Father as to the Lord Jesus, God being the great author of salvation; read the letter as written with a double purpose, an affectionate reminder from an old master to a disciple exposed to great perils; and gloss the word for son as legitimate rather than spurious, while marking the mercy added to the usual greeting as the mark of an old man's deepening tenderness.

Ask why an apostolic title is asserted at all in a private letter, since Timothy needed no proof of it and would have been content with the name, so that the designation must be maintained for other eyes than his; and add that the office is named less for the recipient's sake than for those to whom what follows must come with weight and authority.

Take the word apostle at its bare meaning first, a person sent from one to another with no dignity implied, and then observe what the New Testament makes of it, men sent expressly from God with the message of salvation, which is the highest character a human being can bear; draw from the address that familiarity is to be set aside where the things of God are concerned; and read the last title as the summary of the rest, since without Jesus the world was hopeless and he is called our hope exactly as he is called our life, our peace and our righteousness.

Begin from the office and call the dignity of an apostle great and admirable, noticing that Paul constantly sets out the grounds of it — not as a man taking honour to himself, but as one entrusted with it and under a necessity of saying so.
Count the credentials in the inscription and find them unquestionable, since the writer has not only a commission but a commandment, and that not only from God our Saviour but from Jesus Christ.

debates.question: Was Paul the instrument of Timothy's conversion?

sides.position: Yes: Timothy was converted by his instrumentality, and Paul, having no children of his own, adopted him as a son
No: Timothy was already a converted disciple, well reported of by the brethren, when Paul first met him, so the name of son comes from his youth, from affection, or from later instruction
The relationship is closer than any fleshly one, whatever its origin
It may be settled either way by the rabbinic maxim that he who teaches the law to his neighbour's son is reckoned to have begotten him, though the Greek may equally mean beloved son

outliers.note: Alone asks why an apostolic title should be asserted in a private letter at all, and answers that Timothy needed no such proof, so the designation is maintained for other eyes than his.

Alone reads the salutation as an exercise in not taking honour to oneself, observing that Paul sets out the grounds of his office as a man entrusted with it and under necessity rather than as one claiming it.

themes: my own son in the faith

3.pericope_label: As I besought thee to abide still at Ephesus, when I went into Macedonia, that thou mightest charge some that they teach no other doctrine, Neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions, rather than godly edifying which is in faith: so do. Now the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned: From which some having swerved have turned aside unto vain jangling; Desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm.

schools.summary: Reconstruct the circumstances from the sentence, that Paul and Timothy had worked together at Ephesus and Paul was compelled to leave before finishing, so that what he left behind was a standing commission rather than a single order; date the parting after the first Roman imprisonment and beyond the period covered by the Acts; note that the false teachers are deliberately unnamed because the letter was meant as a public document, though names are given readily enough at the chapter's end; and supply the history of the Jewish oral law, handed down by a succession of teachers, enlarged by famous Rabbis and preserved for centuries by memory or in secret rolls.

Give a motive for the arrangement, that a bad seed had been sown and Paul, obliged to go into Macedonia, wanted a man of tried prudence to stay and stop a pernicious doctrine from spreading; observe that no people ever possessed a greater stock of fables than the Jews and point the reader to the Talmud for them; understand the genealogies as pedigrees that could never be made out in either direction, especially those touching the Messiah and the priesthood; and distinguish these from the genealogies of Scripture, which are not in question.

Turn the word about love into a warning on friendship, that nothing is so injurious to mankind as to undervalue it, and that the neglect of it has been the occasion of all heresies — since men who did not love their brethren came to envy those in high repute, and from envying grew eager for power.

Make the divine law the commandment in view and find its whole scope in engaging us to love God and one another, so that whatever weakens either our love to God or our love to the brethren defeats the end of the commandment itself.

Take the end of the commandment as the design of the charge just given, whose purpose was to keep peace and brotherly love, both of which are hindered by speculative notions, fabulous stories and genealogical contentions; and describe the men who swerved as having erred from the law they professed to honour, missing its end and creating feuds and divisions where they should have promoted love.

debates.question: Had those who swerved ever held what they missed?

sides.position: No: the verb means to miss a mark, and it does not follow that a man who misses one had ever hit it
They had once been in the right direction but did not keep in it, and are still reckoned within the church
They pretended to aim at the mark and missed it

debates.question: What is the commandment whose end is charity?

sides.position: The charge just given to Timothy, whose design was peace and brotherly love
The divine law, whose whole scope is to engage us to love God and one another
Taken by some for the gospel and by others for this particular injunction

outliers.note: Alone traces all heresy to a failure of friendship, arguing that men who did not love their brethren came to envy those in high repute and from envying grew eager for power.

Alone supplies the history of the Jewish oral law behind the charge about fables, handed down by a succession of teachers, enlarged by famous Rabbis, and preserved for centuries by memory or in secret rolls.

8.pericope_label: But we know that the law is good, if a man use it lawfully; Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners, for unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers, For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine; According to the glorious gospel of the blessed God, which was committed to my trust.

schools.summary: Read the concession as a defence against an obvious charge, since a man who presses so hard on teachers of the law will be represented as its enemy; then list the ways the following sentence has been taken — of the ceremonial code, of the denunciatory part of the law, or of law's general office in restraining the wicked — and take the righteous man to mean the Christian in the full sense, justified by faith and sanctified, for whom a code enacted centuries earlier was never framed; note how many terms in the catalogue of offenders are rare or unique, several occurring nowhere else in the New Testament.

Grant the whole Mosaic law rather than a part of it, since even the ceremonial is good as it points to Christ while the moral is holy and just in its own nature, useful to convince unbelievers and to guide believers; put the disputed clause grammatically, that the law is not said to have been made otherwise than for the righteous man but not to lie against him, since he does not transgress it; and read the catalogue of offenders as following the commandments in order, the lawless breaking the first, the ungodly the second, the profane the third.

Guard the term righteous before allowing the sentence, since no man is naturally righteous since Adam and none can be justified by the works of the law, so that the man meant is one made righteous by an imputed righteousness received by faith; limit the concession to the moral law, the ceremonial being by then annulled for its weakness and unprofitableness; and give the reason the gospel is invoked as the standard at the close, that no doctrine is sound but what agrees with it.

debates.question: Which law is conceded to be good?

sides.position: The moral law only, the ceremonial being by then annulled for its weakness and unprofitableness
The whole Mosaic law, the ceremonial as pointing to Christ and the moral as holy in its own nature
The law as God gave it, good in itself and in its tendency, when interpreted according to its own spirit and design
The law used lawfully, that is, used to make men conscious of sin and of deserving punishment

debates.question: In what sense is the law not made for a righteous man?

sides.position: The ceremonial law is meant
The denunciatory part of the law is meant
The chief purpose of law is to restrain the wicked, and it does not lie against a man who does not transgress it
The righteous man is the Christian justified by faith, for whom the Mosaic code was never enacted

outliers.note: Alone reads the catalogue of offenders as following the commandments in order, the lawless breaking the first, the ungodly and sinners the second, the unholy and profane the third.
Alone works the catalogue lexically rather than morally, noting how many of its terms are rare or unique and that one appears to be a late form coined for the occasion.

themes: if a man use it lawfully
not made for a righteous man

12.pericope_label: And I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who hath enabled me, for that he counted me faithful, putting me into the ministry; Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief. And the grace of our Lord was exceeding abundant with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.

schools.summary: Weigh what the word blasphemer can mean here, since the writer was no open blasphemer in the modern sense and no profane swearer, his character having been the reverse; what he had done was to revile the name of Christ and oppose his cause while not believing him the Messiah, and in that opposition he was really guilty; note the cost of the calling, which required abandoning a career of persecution together with every scheme of ambition; and observe that the phrase used for thanking occurs nowhere else in this writer.

Take the word for ministry at its plainest, as the deaconship or service of mankind by preaching, and let the strengthening include the miraculous gifts of the Spirit; gloss the three terms of the confession as speaking impiously of Jesus, exterminating to the utmost of one's power all who called on his name, and being as full of insolence as of malevolence while thinking all the while to do God service; then make the plea of ignorance the hinge, not as excusing the sin but as leaving the sinner capable of mercy, which he would hardly have been had he acted against his own conviction — and note that the text says mercy was had because of ignorance, not because of an unconditional election.

Read the passage as a lesson in humility, remarking that its advantages are generally acknowledged while the thing itself is nowhere found, there being affectation of humble talking enough and to spare; and note that a man conscious of great merits must struggle to be humble, and was the more exposed here because a good conscience swells a man like a gathering humour.

Draw three points about the ministry from the thanksgiving: that putting men into it is Christ's work, since ministers cannot properly make themselves and God condemned the prophets who ran unsent; that whom he calls he qualifies, so that men no way fit for the work were not of his putting into it; and that he gives not ability only but fidelity.

Set the thanksgiving against the men just described, who were fond of being teachers and called doctors of the law, whereas the apostle counted it a high honour and special favour to be a preacher of the gospel, and would not glory in gifts he had not given himself but returns the glory of them to Christ.

debates.question: How strong is the word blasphemer here?

sides.position: Not open blasphemy in the modern sense, since Paul treated sacred things with the utmost respect; he reviled the name of Christ while not believing him the Messiah
Blasphemy in the truest sense of the terrible word, since a man who had seen Stephen die and still panted for the blood of the church knew he was not merely reviling men
Speaking impiously of Jesus, his doctrine, his ways and his followers

debates.question: What does the plea of ignorance do?

sides.position: It is why mercy was extended, Paul having acted under the prejudices of his countrymen, though it does not excuse the conduct

It did not take away the sin but left him capable of mercy, which he would hardly have been had he acted against his own conviction — and the text says mercy came for this reason, not because of an unconditional election

outliers.note: Alone turns the thanksgiving into an essay on humility, remarking that there is affectation of humble talking enough and to spare while humbleness of mind is nowhere to be found, and that a good conscience swells a man like a gathering humour.
Alone uses the plea of ignorance against a doctrine, observing that the text gives ignorance and not unconditional election as the reason mercy was obtained.

15.pericope_label: This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief. Howbeit for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first Jesus Christ might shew forth all longsuffering, for a pattern to them which should hereafter believe on him to life everlasting. Now unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

schools.summary: Identify the opening words as a fixed formula found only in these letters and once at the close of the Apocalypse, used for weighty truths repeated in the assemblies until they became watchwords, in which may be seen the germs of the later creeds; observe that the phrase about Christ coming into the world is Johannine language the writer cannot have read, so that no formal quotation is in view but a saying already current; correct the English word first, which means foremost in guilt rather than earliest in time; and render the word for pattern as a rough outline or sketch.

Take the two epithets in order and give a reason for each, that the saying may be credited without the slightest hesitation because God himself has spoken it and the death of Christ has confirmed it, and that it is worthy of all acceptation because all men are sinners and justly condemned, so that what concerns every man deserves to be received by every man; press the last word of the verse, that Christ came to save sinners without exception; and reduce the purpose of the example to its shortest form, that none might hereafter despair.

Explain why such a formula was needed at all: the favours of God so far exceed human hope that they are often not believed, and a man receiving some great good asks himself whether it is not a dream — what seemed incredible here being that enemies and sinners, justified neither by the law nor by works, should be advanced through faith alone.

Give the formula a polemical edge, set as it is against fables, endless genealogies and contentions about the law, and unfold what the faithfulness consists in: God's faithfulness to himself and to his own perfections, to a law thereby made honourable, to a word of promise now fulfilled, and Christ's faithfulness in carrying the work through.

sides.position: A fixed formula of the early churches, rehearsed until it became a watchword, in which may be seen the germs of the creeds
A definite saying being quoted, in language known from the Fourth Gospel though Paul could not have read it
A doctrine assuredly true and to be depended on, thrown in parenthetically because the writer's mind was full of the subject

outliers.note: Alone identifies the faithful sayings as liturgical watchwords repeated in the assemblies of the first churches, and sees in them the germs of the later creeds.
Alone explains why such a formula was needed, that the favours of God so far exceed human hope that men receiving them ask whether it is not a dream.

18.pericope_label: This charge I commit unto thee, son Timothy, according to the prophecies which went before on thee, that thou by them mightest war a good warfare; Holding faith, and a good conscience; which some having put away concerning faith have made shipwreck: Of whom is Hymeneus and Alexander; whom I have delivered unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme.

schools.summary: Take the prophecies as hopes long entertained of the young man, so that in trusting him the apostle acted in conformity with expectations already cherished; find in the opening verb the image of setting food beside a man and then of entrusting, a banking figure making the charge a deposit lodged for keeping; read the whole as a bequest, the last heritage an old master would leave his favourite disciple; and take the holding of faith as fidelity, the loyalty a good soldier owes, rather than as adherence to a system of doctrine.

Keep prediction and performance apart, since the calling was foretold while the behaviour in it remained contingent on the use made of grace, which is exactly why an exhortation to war a good warfare is added; work the nautical figure hard, with conscience thrust away as a foolhardy soldier throws off shield and breastplate or a mad sailor his pilot, helm and compass; and press the wreck to a conclusion, that none can make shipwreck of faith who never had it, so that these men were once true believers and fell not only foully but finally.

Turn the mention of prophecies into a rule for choosing ministers, since the office is of great dignity and to bring forward a worthy man requires a divine election — had when the choice is made without human passion, looking to no temporal consideration and swayed neither by friendship nor enmity, as the apostles chose Matthias by prayer before they had received the Spirit; and complain that the church has since advanced to the extreme of negligence.

Define the ministry from the charge, as a trust committed to men to see the gospel duly applied according to its Author's design; and take up the figure that follows, that the ministry is a warfare, a good warfare against sin and Satan, waged under the banner of the Captain of our salvation and against his enemies.

Note that the apostle has returned after a digression about his own conversion to the subject he began with, and that the charge includes preaching the gospel himself as well as forbidding others to teach otherwise; take faith here for the body of Christian truth rather than the grace of faith, and make the holding of it a public holding forth in the ministry rather than a bare profession retained without wavering.

debates.question: What were the prophecies that went before on Timothy?

sides.position: Hopes long entertained of him, that he was a man to whom important trusts might be committed
Predictions by inspired men of what he should be, though his behaviour in the calling remained contingent
Words uttered when he was received as an evangelist, probably by many persons

debates.question: Can a man make shipwreck of faith he once had?

sides.position: Yes: none can make shipwreck of faith who never had it, so these were once true believers and fell finally, since ships once wrecked cannot afterwards be saved
What is held is fidelity rather than a system of doctrine, and what was thrust away was the good conscience
Faith here is the body of Christian truth, held forth publicly in the ministry rather than merely professed

outliers.note: Alone turns the verse into a rule for ecclesiastical elections, requiring that a choice be made without human passion and swayed neither by friendship nor enmity, and complaining that the church of his own day has advanced to the extreme of negligence.
Alone presses the shipwreck to a final conclusion, that none can wreck a faith he never had, so that these men were once true believers and fell not only foully but finally.
